E.2.2 Modality specific metrics
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.p1.1] In addition to these general metrics, we introduce multimodality-specific metrics, motivated by the Iso-Energy Assumption and the phenomenology of VLM embeddings. We report:
[id=A5.I6.i1] 1.
[id=A5.I6.i1.p1.1] Probing accuracy paccp_{\mathrm{acc}}, which quantifies how the geometric organization of dictionary atoms aligns with known structures in latent space.
[id=A5.I6.i2] 2.
[id=A5.I6.i2.p1.1] Functional alignment ρ\rho, an instance-level ratio indicating whether cross-modal alignment is carried by bimodal rather than unimodal features.
[id=A5.I6.i3] 3.
[id=A5.I6.i3.p1.1] Functional and Distributional Agreement (FDA), a distribution-level analogue of ρ\rho that checks consistency of this functional role across populations.
[id=A5.I6.i4] 4.
[id=A5.I6.i4.p1.1] δr​@​1\delta_{\mathrm{r@1}}, an interventional measure of how much retrieval recall degrades when unimodal atoms are ablated.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.p3.1] Together, these four views (geometric, functional, distributional, and causal) consistently probe complementary aspects of how features support cross-modal alignment.
While paccp_{\mathrm{acc}} gives a purely geometric measure of consistency between structures in concepts and embeddings, ρ\rho and FDA link the geometric aspect of alignment to the functional behavior of each feature.
ρ\rho and FDA are two sides of the same coin: while ρ\rho operates at the instance level, capturing how cross-modal alignment is distributed across features functionally, FDA operates at the distribution level and shows whether this functional role is consistent with the global geometry of the two modalities, in a way that is more consistent with the Iso-Energy Assumption.
δr​@​1\delta_{\mathrm{r@1}} complements these functional views by providing a causal perspective on whether bimodal features alone are sufficient to maintain alignment.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px1]
Energy.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1] Energy EE gives a measure of the importance of each feature in the dictionary. See Figure 16(a) for a detailed distribution of energy across features and modality.

[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px2]
Modality Score.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.1] Before turning to the metrics themselves, we introduce the modality score, and a binary mask indicating whether a feature is bimodal. The modality score of feature ii is a direct measure of the component-wise Iso-Energy Assumption:
μi=Ei(img)Ei(img)+Ei(txt)∈[0,1]\mu_{i}=\frac{E_{i}^{(\mathrm{img})}}{E_{i}^{(\mathrm{img})}+E_{i}^{(\mathrm{txt})}}\in[0,1].
Values μi≈1\mu_{i}\approx 1 or μi≈0\mu_{i}\approx 0 correspond to image-only and text-only features, while μi≈0.5\mu_{i}\approx 0.5 indicates balanced activation energy across modalities. We refer to the former as unimodal features and the latter as bimodal features. To make this distinction operational, we introduce a binary mask 𝜹i\bm{\delta}_{i} indicating whether feature ii is classified as bimodal. In practice, 𝜹i\bm{\delta}_{i} is obtained by thresholding μi\mu_{i} within an interval [τ,1−τ][\tau,1-\tau] around 0.50.5, with τ=0.05\tau=0.05. We use a bridge-based consistency criterion to define τ\tau, which we introduce later.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px3]
Linear Structure.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px3.p1.1] We evaluate how the geometric organization of dictionary atoms aligns with the known structure of the modality gap. In Figure 2, a linear projection of feature vectors reveals three distinct clusters corresponding to image-only, text-only, and bimodal features. This geometry of concept organization closely aligns with the geometry of embeddings and the modality gap : image–only features are aligned with the image cone, similarly for text, while bimodal features are orthogonal to modality information. We define probing accuracy paccp_{\mathrm{acc}} to quantify how well the geometric structure of concepts aligns with embedding structure and the modality gap. High paccp_{\mathrm{acc}} indicates strong alignment.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px3.p2.1] Each feature DiD_{i} is considered as a linear probe classifying embeddings. Unimodal features are expected to be highly predictive, yielding high accuracy, whereas bimodal features should be domain-agnostic, yielding an accuracy near 0.50.5.
The score sis_{i} of unimodal feature ii is simply its accuracy a​c​cacc. For bimodal features, si=1−2∗(max⁡(acc,1−acc)−0.5)s_{i}=1-2*(\max(\mathrm{acc},1-\mathrm{acc})-0.5) is close to 1 if they are consistently anti-informative (i.e. good at being bad), and close to 00 otherwise.
Finally, paccp_{\mathrm{acc}} is computed as the energy-weighted average of the sis_{i} over all features:
pacc=∑iEi⋅si∑iEip_{\mathrm{acc}}=\frac{\sum_{i}E_{i}\cdot s_{i}}{\sum_{i}E_{i}}.

[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px5]
Functional Alignment.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px5.p1.1] BΣB_{\Sigma} captures functional alignment, the combined functional similarity and geometric alignment of features across modalities. It reflects each feature pair’s contribution to cross-modal alignment under the contrastive objective, with its entries providing pairwise alignment score.
Thus we define ρ\rho the ratio between total BΣB_{\Sigma} bridge score adjacent to bimodal features —i.e. for all pairs (i,j)(i,j) where at least one of ii or jj is a bimodal feature— and that adjacent only to unimodal features —i.e. both ii and jj are unimodal. ρ>1\rho>1 means functional alignment is primarily done by bimodal features; ρ<1\rho<1 means unimodal pairs spuriously carry it.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px6]
Distributional Alignment.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px6.p1.1] In contrast, BΓB_{\Gamma} captures distributional alignment between modalities. Its total mass is 1−c1-c, where cc is the transport cost. The entries of BΓB_{\Gamma} reveal which features contribute to balancing or imbalancing the alignment.
A high BΓ,i,jB_{\Gamma,i,j} indicates features ii and jj jointly contribute to aligning the two distributions. A low score is harder to interpret: it may reflect features contributing to imbalance (if Γi,j≠0\Gamma_{i,j}\neq 0) or unmatched pairs by the transport plan.
Bimodal features should belong to both modalities’ distribution (particularly matching mostly to themselves) and thus drive distributional alignment. On the other hand, unimodal features should be specific to it’s corresponding modality’s distribution and thus should not participate in the overall distributional alignment.
This motivates the Functional and Distributional Agreement (𝐅𝐃𝐀\mathrm{FDA}) ratio:

[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px6.p1.2] Here, α\alpha is the sum of bridge scores adjacent to a bimodal feature, and ε\varepsilon is the proportion of energy in bimodal features.
FDA\mathrm{FDA} is a mirror of the instance–level ρ\rho. It summarizes the impact of bimodal and unimodal features on the distributional alignment between the two modalities. The higher the FDA\mathrm{FDA}, the better the dictionary is at capturing features whose functional behavior consistently matches their geometric distribution across modalities. Indeed, bimodal features should always carry most of the alignment relative to their overall energy.
A low FDA means either bimodal features fail to align distributions properly or unimodal features are spuriously filling this role, indicating a breakdown in the shared conceptual structure.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px7]
Intervention.
[id=A5.SS2.SSS2.Px7.p1.1] After these two functional measures, we turn to the causal behavior of bimodal feature, asking if they alone are sufficient to explain the recall performance of the embeddings. To do so, we define δr​@​1\delta_{\mathrm{r@1}} as the difference in recall between embeddings reconstructed with the full dictionary and those reconstructed by filtering out unimodal features.

Appendix H Semantic vector arithmetic.
[id=A8.p1.1] After training SAEs with desirable properties, based on our hypotheses on the representations of VLM dual encoders, we now ask whether they can be used to improve their performance on downstream tasks. To do so, we select both zero-shot accuracy, measured on ImageNet in Appendix I as part of the modality gap experiment, and retrieval, measured in this section on FashionIQ. See Appendix J for details on this dataset.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
Notations.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] Let Q∈RN×dQ\in R^{N\times d} be query vectors and T∈ℝN×dT\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} be target vectors. The task consists in maximizing average recall on batches bb of cosine similarity matrix Qb⋅Tb⊤Q_{b}\cdot T_{b}^{\top}.
TT are embeddings of target images, and QQ will involve IsrcI_{\mathrm{src}}, source image embeddings, and Δ\Delta, embeddings of relative captions.
Let ZTZ_{T}, ZIsrcZ_{I_{\mathrm{src}}} and ZΔZ_{\Delta} be the sparse codes of T,IsrcT,I_{\mathrm{src}} and Δ\Delta given by our SAE.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1] Let T^≔ZT​D\widehat{T}\coloneqq Z_{T}D be the set of reconstructed activations, and T~≔(ZT⊙𝜹)​D\widetilde{T}\coloneqq(Z_{T}\odot\bm{\delta})D be the set of bimodal activations (recall that D∈ℝK×dD\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d} is the dictionary and 𝜹∈{0,1}K\bm{\delta}\in\{0,1\}^{K} is the binary mask selecting bimodal features, and broadcasted to the size of the codes). Similarly, let I^src\widehat{I}_{\mathrm{src}}, I~src\widetilde{I}_{\mathrm{src}}, Δ^\widehat{\Delta} and Δ~\widetilde{\Delta} be reconstructions and bimodal versions of IsrcI_{\mathrm{src}} and Δ\Delta.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2]
Queries.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] We define the following queries. First, we use QI^srcbaseline≔I^srcQ^{\mathrm{baseline}}_{\widehat{I}_{\mathrm{src}}}\coloneqq\widehat{I}_{\mathrm{src}} and QΔ^baseline≔Δ^Q^{\mathrm{baseline}}_{\widehat{\Delta}}\coloneqq\widehat{\Delta} as lower bounds for any other queries. Then, let Q≔I^src+Δ^Q\coloneqq\widehat{I}_{\mathrm{src}}+\widehat{\Delta} be the classical way of doing semantic vector arithmetic, and QSAE≔I^src+Δ~Q_{\mathrm{SAE}}\coloneqq\widehat{I}_{\mathrm{src}}+\widetilde{\Delta} be arithmetic restricted on bimodal features.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1] See Figure 5 for a visual representation of all vectors involved. Note that queries are scaled to end up on the unit sphere on this representation, the actual result of the addition is indicated with a cross.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px3]
Retrieval.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] We find that QSAEQ_{\mathrm{SAE}} systematically outperforms QQ in terms of retrieval recall, across the six models we tested (Table 8).
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4]
Out of Distribution.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1] We also measure the out of distribution (OOD) score of each of our four queries distribution to the target distribution. The idea is to measure whether our queries actually match targets or are just vectors that happen to be able to do retrieval.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1] We use the distance between QiQ_{i} and it’s K-th nearest neighbor in T^\widehat{T}— similarly for TiT_{i}—then we find the optimal threshold on the distance to classify QQ vs T^\widehat{T}. The final OOD score of Q is the accuracy of this classifier. This approach is popular in the OOD literature (Sun et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022). We typically use K=10K=10. We repeat that procedure for QSAEQ_{\mathrm{SAE}} and the two baselines.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.1] We expect QI^srcbaselineQ^{\mathrm{baseline}}_{\widehat{I}_{\mathrm{src}}} to have the exact same distribution as T^\widehat{T} and QΔ^baselineQ^{\mathrm{baseline}}_{\widehat{\Delta}} to be extremely out of distribution, due to the modality gap. Also due to the modality gap, we expect QQ to be completely OOD. Intuitively, if you only consider unimodal biases, QQ will have the mean of both. As biases are the strongest components of all embeddings, this means that QQ will end up in a cone disjoint from both the image and text embedding distribution. In practice, there are a lot of other unimodal features that are not biases. Thus, by intervening only on shared representations, we should have QSAEQ_{\mathrm{SAE}} end up in the same distribution as T^\widehat{T}.
[id=A8.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p4.1] Results are available in Figure 23 and Table 7. We can see that, as expected, restricting the intervention to shared representations reduces drastically the difference in query and target distribution.

[id=A9]
Appendix I Removing the modality gap
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We investigate two methods and two baselines for removing the modality gap between II and TT. We measure the modality gap using the difference in mean (DiM) and the Wasserstein distance 𝒲\mathcal{W}, and consider the performance in recall on LAION. We also include COCO and ImageNet to study the transferability of our methods on unseen data distributions, and on unseen tasks.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px2]
Notations.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] Let’s first recall some notations. Let II and TT denote image and text embeddings, with respective mean μI\mu_{I} and μT\mu_{T}. Let ZIZ_{I}, ZTZ_{T} be the codes of II, TT given by our SAE. Let DD be the dictionary, and 𝜹∈{0,1}K\bm{\delta}\in\{0,1\}^{K} be the binary mask selecting bimodal features, and broadcasted to the size of the codes.
Let I^≔ZI​D\widehat{I}\coloneqq Z_{I}D be the set of reconstructed activations, and I~≔(ZI⊙𝜹)​D\widetilde{I}\coloneqq(Z_{I}\odot\bm{\delta})D, and similarly for T^\widehat{T} and T~\widetilde{T}.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px3]
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] Our first method comes from the analysis of our SAEs : we remove unimodal concepts, ending up with I~\widetilde{I} and T~\widetilde{T}. This is the only method that doesn’t enforce the mean of the two distribution to exactly match. Instead, we rely on our SAEs to capture all shared representations. As a baseline we propose to consider the centered versions of the data Icenter≔I^−𝝁𝑰^I_{\mathrm{center}}\coloneqq\widehat{I}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{I}}} and Tcenter≔T^−𝝁𝑻^T_{\mathrm{center}}\coloneqq\widehat{T}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{T}}}. The motivation for this baseline is the observation in Appendix F that unimodal features are predominantly small variations around a unique direction, except for small energy ones which are orders of magnitude less energetic.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1] For the above baseline and the next two methods, we use reconstructed embeddings instead of the original ones for fairness of comparison, as SAEs never perfectly reconstruct activations. Additionally, for the means, we use the means on the LAION dataset even on COCO and on ImageNet, also for fairness, as SAEs were trained on the LAION dataset.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px4]
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1] The second method is called embedding shift in Liang et al. (2022), and it essentially consist in the following transformation : Ishift≔I^−𝝁𝑰^+𝝁𝑰^+𝝁𝑻^𝟐I_{\mathrm{shift}}\coloneqq\widehat{I}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{I}}}+\bm{\frac{\mu_{\widehat{I}}+\mu_{\widehat{T}}}{2}} and Tshift≔T^−𝝁𝑻^+𝝁𝑰^+𝝁𝑻^𝟐T_{\mathrm{shift}}\coloneqq\widehat{T}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{T}}}+\bm{\frac{\mu_{\widehat{I}}+\mu_{\widehat{T}}}{2}}. We propose the following baseline for this method : we replace the average of the means by a random direction 𝒓\bm{r}, sampled uniformly from the unit sphere—Irand≔I^−𝝁𝑰^+𝒓I_{\mathrm{rand}}\coloneqq\widehat{I}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{I}}}+\bm{r} and Trand≔T^−𝝁𝑻^+𝒓T_{\mathrm{rand}}\coloneqq\widehat{T}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{T}}}+\bm{r}.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1] These two methods are not comparable to the first two in terms of modality gap, as even if the DiM is similar, the Wasserstein distance 𝒲\mathcal{W} behaves very differently. Indeed, in the first two methods, data is centered around 00 and is roughly uniformly spread on the unit sphere. On the other hand, by manually adding a mean, these methods concentrate the data on a narrow cone, significantly reducing the 𝒲\mathcal{W}. We illustrate these four methods on synthetic 3D points in Figure 24.
Figure 24: Illustration of the four methods to remove the modality gap on synthetic data points.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px5]
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1] Results are compiled in Tables 9, 10 and 11. We can see that the shift method introduced in previous work is by far the worst, significantly reducing recall performances, then comes the random baseline. The mean baseline outperforms the concept-based approach in terms of recall, but it does not close the modality gap.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.1] We also indicate in Figure 25 the KNN distance histograms for our four methods, following the OOD detection method described in Appendix H, for the CLIP-L model on the LAION dataset. We take the image distribution as the reference one, and the text distribution as the ”OOD” one. This illustrates a bit more precisely the effect of all methods on the distribution of embeddings. We can see that our method is the only one that closes the gap by merging the two distributions.
